newsitem.title: USA: Corruption charges dropped against ex-Miami manager.
newsitem.headline: Corruption charges dropped against ex-Miami manager.

text.p: Federal prosecutors on Wednesday dropped corruption and embezzlement charges against former City Manager Cesar Odio in a surprise denoument of a scandal which stunned Miami.

Odio pleaded guilty to a remaining charge of obstructing justice for which he faces a maximum sentence of between 10-16 months in prison, his attorney Ed Shohat said. He had faced a maximum 35 years imprisonment and $1.5 million in fines if found guilty on the other charges.

"I feel better in the sense that my family has been under tremendous strain," Odio said on the steps of the downtown courthouse after a brief appearance before U.S. District Judge K. Michael Moore. "I have not let anyone down."

Odio, 61, resigned as city manager after he was indicted in October on charges of trying to solicit a kickback from an insurance company that sought a city contract. In a six-count indictment he and lobbyist Jorge de Cardenas were accused of conspiracy, embezzlement and witness tampering.
Shohat said Wednesday the corruption and bribery charges were dropped as result of bargaining with the government.

The so-called Operation Green Palm investigation into misuse of public finances brought the downfall of city commissioner Miller Dawkins. He pleaded guilty to accepting a $75,000 bribe from a computer company and is scheduled to begin a 27-month prison sentence in June.
The scandal rocked Miami and badly dented its hard-won efforts to show it was a good place to do business in as well as have fun. In its wake it emerged that Miami was running a $68 million deficit.

And just as the city was getting back in its stride, two weeks ago it emerged that the Port of Miami was running a $22 million deficit while its funds were spent on Super Bowl tickets, luxury car hires and campaign contributions to county commissioners. Port director Carmen Lunetta resigned as result of those revelations.
Odio, a hero to Miami's Cuban exile and immigrant population, had always professed his innocence.

He arrived in Miami from communist-ruled Cuba in 1961 and in his 11 years as city manager he steered the city through several crises, including the arrival of waves of Cuban boatpeople and the devastating Hurricane Andrew in 1992.
"He is a very proud man who has worked long and hard for the city of Miami," Shohat said outside the courthouse. "It is a day of mixed emotion. He's happy to have it all behind him."

The case also exposed raw racial nerves in this melting-pot city. Many Cuban Americans accused the "Anglo" establishment of trying to demolish an immigrant success story. Anglos said it showed Cubans had brought Latin American-style corruption and patronage to city politics.
Shohat gave no details of the plea agreement but dismissed a reporter's suggestion it was a "sweetheart" deal.
The obstruction of justice charge related to an effort to persuade former city finance director Manohar Surana not to give evidence.
Surana, who agreed to carry an FBI wire tap, secretly recorded a conversation in which Odio allegedly counted out money received from de Cardenas. Surana has pleaded guilty to unspecified charges.
Odio's sentencing was set for Aug 20. He had been scheduled to go on trial on Aug. 4. --U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
